s: Belus, son of Libya and Poseidon and twin brother of Agenor, remained in Egypt, reigned over the Egyptians, married Anchinoe, daughter of Nile, and fathered the twins Egyptus and Danaus.
Agenor went to Phoenicia, where he married Telephassa and had Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix.

Egyptus, son of Belus and Anchinoe and twin of Danaus, was settled in Arabia, conquered the Melampods’ country, and fathered fifty sons, who later came to Argos seeking marriage with Danaus’s daughters.

Danaus, son of Belus and Anchinoe and twin brother of Egyptus, was a former king of Argos and father of fifty daughters by many wives. Fearing Egyptus’s sons after a kingdom quarrel, he built the first ship on Athena’s advice, fled with his daughters, touched Rhodes, and set up an image of Lindian Athena. At Argos he received the kingdom from Gelanor, named its inhabitants Danai, and directed his daughters’ marriages and remarriages.

are_married_to daughters of Danaus [marriages arranged by lot] The fifty sons of Egyptus came to Argos, asked Danaus to end the hostility, and sought to marry his daughters. Danaus allotted the marriages among them, but the sons were killed by their brides while they slept, except for Lynceus.

The daughters of Danaus fled with Danaus to Argos, were given as brides, and all but Hypermnestra killed their sleeping bridegrooms. They buried and honored the dead, were purified by Athena and Hermes, and later had their marriages awarded through an athletic contest.
Rhodes received Althaemenes and Apemosyne after they left Crete. Catreus later came to Rhodes intending to transfer his kingdom to Althaemenes, but Althaemenes killed him unknowingly there.
Amymone, a daughter of Danaus, searches drought-stricken country for water, accidentally angers a satyr, and is rescued by Poseidon. Poseidon shows her Lerna’s springs; they marry and have Nauplius.
is_mother_of Pentheus [with Echion] Agave was the mother of Pentheus. In a fit of madness on Cithaeron, she mistook Pentheus for a wild beast and tore him limb from limb.
Busiris, son of Poseidon and Lysianassa, institutes annual sacrifices of strangers to Zeus on an oracle’s advice during Egypt’s dearth, but Hercules kills him after being captured.

l: mass killing of the bridegrooms, The Library
s: is_a killing of the sons of Egyptus [by the daughters of Danaus while the bridegrooms slept] After Danaus agreed to the marriages, he gave his daughters daggers, and they killed the sons of Egyptus while the bridegrooms slept. Hypermnestra alone did not participate, because she spared Lynceus; the other daughters buried the bridegrooms’ heads at Lerna and honored their bodies before the city.

Catreus was a son of Minos and father of Aerope, Clymene, Apemosyne, and Althaemenes. An oracle said that one of his children would kill him, and Althaemenes later killed him unknowingly when Catreus came to Rhodes.
Hesione, daughter of Laomedon, is fastened to rocks for a sea monster but rescued by Hercules; after Heracles captures the city, she is awarded to Telamon.

Acrisius is king of Argos, twin brother of Proetus, husband of Eurydice, and father of Danae, making him Perseus’s grandfather. After an oracle foretells Danae’s son would kill him, he confines Danae and casts her and Perseus into the sea in a chest. Fleeing Argos in fear, he is accidentally killed by Perseus and buried outside the city.

Proetus, twin brother of Acrisius, returns from Lycia and becomes king of Tiryns. Restored by his father-in-law, he fathers children, accepts Melampus’s cure terms, and later seeks Bellerophon’s death through Iobates.

Iobates, king of Lycia and father of Philonoe, receives Bellerophon with Proetus’s death order but sets him deadly tasks instead. After Bellerophon succeeds, Iobates reveals the letter, gives him Philonoe, and leaves him the kingdom at death.
has_spouse Proetus Stheneboea fell in love with Bellerophon and sent him proposals for a meeting. When he rejected them, she falsely told Proetus that Bellerophon had made improper advances to her.
Tiryns, a Cyclops-fortified city, became Proetus’s realm after restoration and Argive division, then the place where Hercules lived while serving Eurystheus for twelve years.

daughter_of Acrisius [by Eurydice] Danae was confined by Acrisius in a brazen chamber. She was seduced by Proetus according to one account, or had intercourse with Zeus in the form of gold according to another, and gave birth to Perseus.

dwell_by Thermodon [as a warlike people] The Amazons dwell around the Thermodon and are described as a large, warlike people. After Hera claims that the visiting strangers will abduct their queen, the Amazons ride armed toward Hercules's ship, fight him, and are defeated.

Medusa is a Gorgon and the only mortal one. While she slept, Perseus, guided by Athena and using a brazen shield to view her image, beheaded her. Afterward Pegasus and Chrysaor, her children by Poseidon, sprang from her body; in Hades she appears as an empty phantom.
is_a winged horse [offspring of Medusa and Poseidon] Pegasus was a winged horse born from Medusa and Poseidon. Bellerophon rode Pegasus into the air and used the height to shoot down the Chimera.

l: madness of the Argive women, The Library
s: Proetus's daughters went mad because, according to Hesiod, they refused the rites of Dionysus, or, according to Acusilaus, because they disparaged the wooden image of Hera. Their madness spread to the other women, who abandoned their homes, destroyed their children, and went into the desert.

Melampus promised to cure the maddened women through drugs and purifications in return for a share of the sovereignty. During the pursuit to Sicyon, Iphinoe died, while the other daughters were purified and recovered their wits.

Proetus gave Bellerophon a letter to carry to Iobates, and the letter ordered Iobates to kill Bellerophon. Iobates showed the letter to Bellerophon only after Bellerophon had completed the assigned campaigns.

Iobates ordered Bellerophon to kill the Chimera, fight the Solymi, fight the Amazons, and ambush the reputedly bravest Lycians. Bellerophon completed every task and killed the enemies sent against him.
The nymphs possess winged sandals, a wallet, and the cap of Hades, and give Perseus this sought equipment after the Phorcides direct him to them.
Geryon, son of Chrysaor and Callirrhoe, inhabits Erythia, has three joined male bodies, and owns red kine; when Hercules takes them, Geryon attacks beside Anthemus and is shot dead.
Ethiopia was ruled by Cepheus. Perseus arrived there and found Andromeda exposed as food for a sea monster.

Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiepea, was first betrothed to Phineus. During a calamity, she was exposed as sea-monster prey and bound to a rock. Perseus saw and loved her, killed the monster, rescued and married her, and had children with her.
Cassiopeia, wife of Cepheus and mother of Andromeda, claimed to be more beautiful than the Nereids. The Nereids became angry because of this claim.
The sea monster was sent against the land by Poseidon. It was to receive Andromeda as food after the oracle of Ammon declared that this would end the disaster.
The Delphic oracle gives Acrisius a prophecy, names Alcides Hercules, and directs his Tiryns residence, service, labours, and immortality.
is_washed_ashore_on Seriphus Acrisius put Danae and Perseus into a chest and cast it into the sea. The chest was washed ashore on Seriphus, where Dictys took it up.
The winged sandals belonged to the nymphs. Perseus received them from the nymphs and fitted them to his ankles.
The wallet, called the kibisis, belonged to the nymphs and was used for carrying the Gorgon’s head. Perseus received it and slung it around himself.

Gorgon’s head is Medusa’s head, taken after her beheading and carried by Perseus in a wallet. Ordered by Polydectes, Perseus uses it to turn Phineus, conspirators, Polydectes, and his friends to stone, then gives it to Athena for her shield.

l: the prophecy about Acrisius, The Library
s: A prophecy concerning Acrisius foretells that Danae will bear Perseus, who will kill him; fearing it, Acrisius confines Danae.

l: Danae’s seduction by Zeus, The Library
s: Danae’s seduction is attributed to Zeus, who became gold and poured into her lap, producing Perseus; some instead say Proetus seduced her.

l: the casting of Danae and Perseus into the sea, The Library
s: Acrisius put Danae and Perseus into a chest and cast them into the sea because he had learned that Danae had borne Perseus.

l: Perseus’s quest for the Gorgon’s head, The Library
s: Polydectes orders Perseus to seek the Gorgon’s head; after Perseus accepts, Hermes and Athena guide him and nymphs provide needed equipment.

l: the decapitation of Medusa, The Library
s: Perseus decapitated the sleeping Medusa while looking at her image in a bronze shield and following Athena’s direction. Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from Medusa after her head was cut off.
Electryon ruled Mycenae, fathered Alcmena and Licymnius, entrusted the kingdom and Alcmena to Amphitryon before war against the Teleboans, and was accidentally killed by Amphitryon.
Menoeceus, Creon’s son, hears Tiresias’s prophecy and kills himself before the gates as an offering to Ares, enabling Theban victory.
The Tafian islands could not be conquered while Pterelaus was alive. After Comaetho removed the golden lock from his head, Pterelaus died and Amphitryon conquered the islands.

Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus and born seven months before the expected birth of Heracles, is the commander who orders and imposes Hercules’s labours. He begins by demanding the Nemean lion’s hide and, frightened by Hercules’s prowess, bars him from Mycenae and requires displays outside its gates, hiding in a bronze jar. He uses Copreus as herald, assigns successive labours, and controls their count: he rejects the hydra because Iolaus helped and rejects tasks done for hire, while receiving the Cretan Bull and mares. He receives and sacrifices Geryon’s red kine to Hera, then orders an eleventh labour for golden apples and receives them. Later he demands the surrender of Hercules’s sons and threatens war; after his own sons are killed, he flees but is pursued and killed by Hyllus, and his head is given to Alcmena.

Alcmena is given to Amphitryon with a kingdom, under Electryon’s requirement that she remain a virgin until his return. She makes marriage depend on Amphitryon avenging her brothers’ deaths. She becomes mother of Heracles/Hercules by Zeus and Iphicles by Amphitryon, later marries Rhadamanthys after Amphitryon’s death, and gouges Eurystheus’s eyes after Hyllus brings his severed head.
A vixen ravages Cadmea and cannot be caught; pursued by Laelaps, it ends when Zeus turns both animals into stones.

Mycenae is a city ruled first by Eurystheus, then by Perseus after fortifying it, and later by Electryon until his death; Eurystheus resides there and has Hercules display captured beasts before its gates.
The Cadmea was ravaged by the Teumessian vixen. Creon required Amphitryon to rid it of the animal before he would assist in the expedition against the Teleboans.

is_a beheading [performed by Perseus with Athena’s guidance] Medusa’s beheading was carried out by Perseus with Athena guiding his hand while he looked at her image in a brazen shield. Some accounts in the text say that Medusa was beheaded for Athena’s sake because the Gorgon had wished to compete with Athena in beauty.
Andromeda’s rescue begins when Perseus promises Cepheus to kill the sea monster for marriage to Andromeda; he kills it, frees her, and faces Phineus’s plot.

is_a death [of Acrisius caused by Perseus] The death of Acrisius occurred during athletic games held by Teutamides of Larissa. Perseus, competing in the pentathlon, accidentally struck Acrisius’s foot with a quoit and killed him, fulfilling the oracle.

is_a death [caused by Amphitryon’s rebounding club] The death of Electryon occurred when Amphitryon threw a club at a cow that had charged while the cattle were being recovered. The club rebounded from the cow’s horns and struck Electryon’s head, killing him.
are_defeated_by Amphitryon [in an expedition against them] The Teleboans were the target of Amphitryon’s expedition, which he undertook after agreeing to avenge Alcmena’s brothers.

l: expedition against the Teleboans, The Library
s: Amphitryon undertook the expedition against the Teleboans and invited Creon to assist him. He also promised a share of the spoils to those who joined him.

The Thebans are people of Thebes facing battle. Armed and organized by Eteocles, they seek Tiresias’s counsel and learn that victory requires Menoeceus’s self-sacrifice to Ares; records also note the monthly exposure of a citizen’s son to a vixen.
Laelaps, a dog brought by Cephalus from Crete, was fated to catch everything it pursued; while hunting the vixen, it chased until Zeus turned both animals to stone.

l: hunt for the vixen, The Library
s: uses Laelaps [the dog brought by Procris from Crete] Amphitryon went to Athens and persuaded Cephalus to join the hunt with the dog Laelaps. The hunt ended when Zeus turned the pursuing dog and the vixen into stones.

l: petrification of the vixen and dog, The Library
s: Laelaps pursues the Teumessian vixen until Zeus turns both the vixen and the dog into stones.

The Tafian islands were attacked by Amphitryon with allies from Athens, Phocis, Argos, and Thebes. After Pterelaus died, Amphitryon conquered all the islands and distributed them among his companions.
Comaetho, daughter of Pterelaus and lover of Amphitryon, removes her father’s golden lock; after Pterelaus dies, Amphitryon kills her.

l: golden lock of Pterelaus, The Library
s: is_on Pterelaus [on his head] The golden lock was taken from Pterelaus’s head by his daughter Comaetho. Its removal caused Pterelaus to die.

l: conquest of the Tafian islands, The Library
s: Amphitryon’s conquest of the Tafian islands became possible after Comaetho removed the golden lock from Pterelaus’s head and Pterelaus died. Amphitryon then gave the islands as spoils to Cephalus and his other allies.
is_performed_by Amphitryon [after the conquest of the Tafian islands] After Comaetho caused Pterelaus’s death by removing the golden lock, Amphitryon killed her.

Tiresias is a blind Theban soothsayer, son of Everes and the nymph Chariclo, with prophetic power, long life, a cornel-wood staff, and understanding of every bird note. He became a woman after wounding copulating snakes on Cyllene and a man again after seeing them again. Hera blinded him, while Zeus gave him soothsaying. He told the Thebans they would win if Menoeceus sacrificed himself to Ares, later advised them to send a herald to the Argives and flee, and died after drinking at Tilphussa spring during that flight.
Born to Europa after Zeus joined her in Crete, Rhadamanthys made laws for islanders, fled to Boeotia, married Alcmena, and after death judged in Hades with Minos.
Cithaeron is a mountain where Bacchanals rave, Pentheus spies and is torn apart, Niobe's male children hunt before Apollo kills them, and Tydeus delivers a succession message.

Iolaus is Hercules’ charioteer and helper, identified with Sardinian inhabitants. He drives Hercules to Lerna, helps defeat the hydra by burning severed heads’ roots, and thereby causes Eurystheus to reject the labour as not completed alone.

l: the madness of Hercules, The Library
s: is_caused_by Hera [through divine jealousy] The madness of Hercules is attributed to Hera’s jealousy and occurs after the battle with the Minyans. During it, Hercules throws his own children by Megara and two children of Iphicles into a fire.

l: the killing of Hercules' children, The Library
s: is_caused_by the madness of Hercules [Hercules threw his children into the fire] The killing of Hercules' children occurs during his madness after the battle with the Minyans. Hercules also kills two children of Iphicles and thereafter condemns himself to exile.

l: the labours of Hercules, The Library
s: The labours of Hercules are tasks initially numbered ten, imposed by Eurystheus and to be performed at Tiryns; their completion is said to bring immortality. The first five are the Nemean lion, Lernaean hydra, Cerynitian hind, Erymanthian boar, and Augean cattle. Eurystheus excludes the hydra because Iolaus helped. After eight years and a month, he assigns an eleventh labour.

The Nemean lion is an invulnerable beast begotten by Typhon. After Eurystheus orders Hercules to bring its hide, Hercules hunts it, drives it into its two-mouthed cave, blocks one entrance, chokes it through the other, and carries its body to Mycenae.

l: the Nemean lion labour, The Library
s: The Nemean lion labour is the first task assigned to Hercules by Eurystheus. Hercules must bring back the lion’s hide and goes to Cleonae, where he stays with Molorchus before hunting it.

A huge creature bred in the swamp of Lerna, the Lernaean hydra ravages cattle and countryside. It has nine heads, including an immortal middle head. During Hercules and Iolaus's defeat of it, a huge crab aids it; its immortal head is buried beneath a rock and its gall used on arrows.
The Cerynitian hind, a golden-horned animal sacred to Artemis at Oenoe, is pursued for a year, captured alive near Ladon, then carried to Mycenae.
A wild boar from Mount Erymanthus ravages Psophis until Hercules pursues, nooses, and carries it alive to Mycenae.
Psophis received Alcmaeon when he came to Phegeus for purification. Later, after the sons of Alcmaeon killed Phegeus and his wife, the Psophidians pursued them but were defeated and fled.

Nessus is a centaur who operates a paid ferry across the Evenus, claiming divine authorization for his justice. While ferrying Deianeira, he attempts to assault her. Hercules shoots him through the heart, and, dying, Nessus deceives Deianeira by giving instructions to use his blood as a love charm.
The Augean cattle belong to Augeias, who has many herds. Eurystheus orders Hercules to remove their dung in a single day.

requires_removal_of dung [in a single day] The fifth labour requires Hercules to carry out the dung from Augeas's cattle-yard in a single day. Hercules completes it by diverting the Alpheus and Peneus through the yard, but Eurystheus does not accept it because Hercules had undertaken it for a promised reward.

targets Stymphalian birds [to chase them away] The sixth labour requires Hercules to chase away the Stymphalian birds. Athena gives him brazen castanets, which he uses to frighten the birds into flight so that he can shoot them.
The Stymphalian birds gather in the wooded lake at Stymphalus, fearing attack by wolves. The sound of Athena's brazen castanets drives them into the air, where Hercules shoots them.

requires_retrieval_of Cretan Bull The seventh labour requires Hercules to bring the Cretan Bull. He captures it after Minos tells him to fight for it himself, brings it to Eurystheus, and then releases it.

The Cretan Bull is an animal from Crete, variously identified as the bull that ferried Europa for Zeus or one Poseidon sent from the sea. It rose at Minos’s request as proof of his kingdom, but Minos kept it instead of sacrificing it; Poseidon made it savage and caused Pasiphae to desire it. After Hercules released it, it wandered through Sparta and Arcadia to Marathon, harming inhabitants. A bull also reached Eryx after swimming from Rhegium and was mingled with Eryx’s herds.

Europa, daughter of Agenor and Telephassa in one account, though possibly Phoenix’s daughter, is loved and carried by Zeus as a tame bull across the sea to Crete. Zeus fathers Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys with her. Her disappearance prompts her brothers’ search; Asterius later marries her and raises her children.

requires_retrieval_of man-eating mares [belonging to Diomedes] The eighth labour requires Hercules to bring the mares of Diomedes to Mycenae. He captures them, but they kill Abderus while he is guarding them; Hercules then kills Diomedes, subdues the Bistones, and delivers the mares to Eurystheus.

kill Abderus [by dragging him after them] The man-eating mares belong to Diomedes and are kept at their mangers. They kill Abderus by dragging him after them, are brought by Hercules to Eurystheus, and are later released and destroyed by wild beasts on Mount Olympus.

requires_retrieval_of belt of Ares [belonging to Hippolyte] The ninth labour requires Hercules to bring Hippolyte's belt. He sails with volunteer comrades to the Amazons, reaches Themiscyra, and takes the belt after killing Hippolyte and fighting the Amazons.
Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, holds Ares’ belt as supremacy’s token; at Themiscyra she promises it to Hercules, but Hera’s incitement sparks suspicion and Hercules kills her.
The belt of Ares belongs to Hippolyte and signifies her superiority over all the Amazons. Hercules obtains it after killing Hippolyte during the conflict at Themiscyra.

Laomedon is presented as Troy’s ruler and as a son of Hercules by Meline. After Apollo and Poseidon fortify Pergamum, he withholds their wages; divine anger brings plague and a sea monster. He exposes his daughter Hesione, then refuses Hercules’s payment. He attacks the ships, kills Oicles, is repelled and besieged, and when the city is captured Heracles shoots him.

are_withheld_by Laomedon [after Pergamum was fortified] Laomedon promised wages to Apollo and Poseidon for fortifying Pergamum but refused to pay them. Hercules also expected payment after rescuing Hesione, but Laomedon refused to give it.

snatches_away people of the plain [carried up by a flood] Poseidon sent the sea monster after Laomedon refused to pay. Carried inland by a flood, it snatched away the people of the plain, and Hesione was exposed to it until Hercules killed it.

are_given_by Zeus [to Tros as compensation for Ganymede's abduction] The horses of Tros were promised to Hercules as payment for rescuing Hesione. The text states that Zeus had given them as a penalty for the abduction of Ganymede.

Sarpedon, son of Poseidon and brother of Poltys, is described as born to Europa after Zeus came together with her in Crete; Homer instead names Zeus and Laodamia. After quarrelling with Minos over Miletus, he fled, allied with Cilix, became king of Lycia, and received three generations’ life from Zeus.
Hercules undertakes Hesione's rescue for Tros's horses and secures it by killing the sea monster, paralleling Perseus and Andromeda's maiden-rescue pattern.

l: tenth labour of Hercules, The Library
s: requires_fetching red kine of Geryon [from Erythia] The tenth labour of Hercules is to fetch the kine of Geryon from Erythia.

Callirrhoe, the daughter of Achelous, became Alcmaeon's wife after his purification by Achelous. She demanded the necklace and robe and, after Alcmaeon's death, asked that her sons by Alcmaeon become full-grown so that they could avenge him.

l: red kine of Geryon, The Library
s: Geryon's red cattle, guarded, are taken by Hercules from Erythia, scatter and are recovered en route, then sacrificed to Hera by Eurystheus.
is_ruled_by Antaeus [at the time of Hercules's passage] Hercules traverses Libya while seeking the golden apples. At that time, Libya is ruled by Antaeus.
The Sun gives Hercules a golden goblet after admiring his courage. Hercules uses it to cross the ocean to Erythia and later returns it to the Sun at Tartessus.
Eryx, son of Poseidon and king of the Elymi, refuses Hercules the escaped bull, is defeated three times in wrestling, and killed.
requires_fetching golden apples [from the Hesperides] The eleventh labour was the task of fetching golden apples from the Hesperides.

The golden apples are gifts associated with Hera’s marriage to Zeus, presented by Earth; another account says they came from Aphrodite. They are located at Atlas among the Hyperboreans, not in Libya, and guarded by the Hesperides and an immortal dragon. In one account Atlas brings three to Hercules, who gives them to Eurystheus; in another Hercules kills the guardian snake and plucks them. Later, Melanion uses them in his race against Atalanta, who stops to pick them up and loses.
The Hesperides are named Aegle, Erytheia, and Arethusa; after eight labours, they guarded the golden apples with an immortal dragon.

l: dragon of the Hesperides, The Library
s: An immortal, hundred-headed dragon, offspring of Typhon and Echidna, uses many varied voices to guard the golden apples; after eight labours had been performed, it is described in this role.
Antaeus, Poseidon's son and king of Libya, kills strangers by wrestling and gains strength from earth until Hercules lifts, breaks, and kills him.

Cerberus is a dog and underworld guardian with three dog heads, a serpent or dragon tail, and many snake heads on his back. In Hercules’ twelfth labor, Pluto allows Hercules to take him without weapons. Hercules masters him at Acheron’s gates, carries him to Eurystheus, then returns him to Hades.
performs Eleusinian initiation [for Hercules after cleansing him] Eumolpus received Hercules at Eleusis and purified him from the killing of the Centaurs. Afterward, Hercules was initiated.

exclude foreigners [at that time] The Eleusinian Mysteries were not then open to foreigners. Hercules could not initially see them because he had not been purified from the killing of the Centaurs, but after Eumolpus purified him, he was initiated.
is_in Laconia [in the region of Laconia] Tainaron in Laconia was the place to which Hercules came after his initiation.

l: twelfth labor of Hercules, The Library
s: The twelfth labor of Hercules was to bring Cerberus from Hades.
Oechalia is attacked and captured by Hercules after he gathers an army to punish Eurytus. Its city is pillaged, and Iole is taken captive.
Iole, daughter of Eurytus, is captured by Hercules at Oechalia; later he charges Hyllus to marry her in adulthood.
Calydon was the place where Hercules wooed and married Deianira. Its people later campaigned with Hercules against Thesprotous.

l: the city of Troy, The Library
s: Heracles's forces besieged the city after Laomedon was driven back. Telamon entered first through a breach in the wall, Heracles followed, and Heracles then captured the city.
After recovering from his illness following the sacrifice, Heracles sailed to Ilium with eighteen penteconters. He brought an army of distinguished men who willingly wanted to campaign.

is_established_by Hercules [after Laomedon was repulsed] After Laomedon killed Oicles and was driven back by Heracles's men, Laomedon was besieged. During the siege, Telamon broke through the wall and entered first, followed by Heracles.
Heracles captured Ilium after entering it behind Telamon. He shot Laomedon and his sons except Podarces and awarded Hesione to Telamon.
Lacedaemon is the second territory assigned in the drawing of lots. Its sign is a serpent, interpreted by the seers as indicating rulers who would be terrible in attack.
Argives are an armed group led by seven leaders that approaches and fights at Thebes, threatening Tegea if Cepheus leaves. After Zeus strikes Capaneus and many fall, they suffer rout and flee.

Auge, daughter of Aleus and priestess of Athena, is seduced by Heracles and secretly bears Telephus, hiding him in Athena’s precinct. When the hidden birth is revealed amid barrenness in the land, Aleus gives her to Nauplius to be killed or sold abroad. Nauplius instead brings her to Teuthras in Mysia, who receives and marries her.
Athena’s precinct, where priestess Auge hid her baby Telephus, became barren; oracles exposed the impiety, prompting the baby’s discovery and Auge’s punishment.
Teuthras, prince and ruler of Mysia and Teuthrania, marries Auge, adopts her son Telephus, and is succeeded as ruler of Mysia by Telephus after his death.

produces whatever is asked for [bestowed by Zeus on the nymphs who reared him] Amalthea’s horn was given by Achelous in exchange for the horn Hercules had broken off. According to Pherecydes, it could supply whatever meat or drink was desired in abundance.
Hercules campaigned against Thesprotous with the Calydonians and captured a city ruled by Phylas. He remained among the Thesprotous and sent sons to Thebes and Sardinia for colonization.
Eunomus, son of Architeles and kinsman of Oeneus, is killed by Hercules while pouring water on his hands.
At a feast with Oeneus, Hercules accidentally struck and killed Eunomus while he poured water on Hercules’s hands, leading Hercules to undergo exile.

Trachis is the destination to which Hercules travels with Deianira, where Ceyx receives him. Hercules later returns to Trachis after being afflicted by the poisoned tunic. Trachis was the place the sons of Hercules left when they fled from Eurystheus through Greece.

l: Nessus's attempted assault on Deianeira, The Library
s: is_attempted_by Nessus Nessus attempted to assault Deianeira while ferrying her across Evenus. Deianeira cried out, and Hercules became aware of what was happening.

l: Heracles's shooting of Nessus, The Library
s: wounds Nessus [in the heart] After hearing Deianeira cry out during Nessus's attempted assault, Heracles shot Nessus in the heart with an arrow. As Nessus was about to die, he spoke to Deianeira about making a love charm for Hercules from his blood and material from his wound.

is_presented_as love charm [by Nessus] Nessus tells Deianira to mix his blood with the seed he dropped and preserve it as a love charm. Deianira later smears it on Hercules's tunic, where it carries the Hydra's poison.

l: love charm for Hercules, The Library
s: is_made_from Nessus's blood [mixed with the seed Nessus had dropped] The supposed love charm consists of material associated with Nessus's blood and the seed he dropped on the ground. Deianira believes it will make Hercules love her, but it instead causes the destruction of his body when applied to his tunic.

contains Hydra's poison [the poison corrodes Hercules's skin when the tunic is warmed] Deianira smears the tunic with what she believes is a love charm before Hercules wears it for a sacrifice. When it is warmed, the Hydra's poison causes it to cling to Hercules's body and tear away his flesh when he removes it.
comes_from Hydra The Hydra's poison is present in the material from Nessus's wound. When the treated tunic is warmed, the poison corrodes Hercules's skin and brings about his death.
Mount Oeta, in Trachinian territory, is where Hercules, afflicted by the tunic, orders and constructs a pyre before being carried up to heaven.

Hercules orders a pyre to be made on Mount Oeta and asks someone to set it alight. No one initially agrees, but Poeas lights it while passing by in search of his flocks. Hercules constructed the pyre on Oeta and ordered it to be kindled. When no one else would light it, Poeas set it alight while Hercules mounted it.

Hyllus, elder son of Hercules by Deianira, marries Iole as Hercules commands. He kills the fleeing Eurystheus near the Scironian cliffs and gives Eurystheus's severed head to Alcmena. Seeking the Heraclids' return, he consults Delphi, returns after three years with an army, is defeated, and killed.
Hercules's death follows the corrosion of his body by the Hydra's poison in the tunic. He is taken to the pyre on Mount Oeta, which is set alight, and a cloud with thunder carries him to heaven.
After the pyre burns, Hercules is carried to heaven in a cloud accompanied by thunder. He receives immortality and is reconciled with Hera.
Hercules captures Oechalia with the aid of Arcadians, Melians from Trachis, and Epicnemidian Locrians. He kills Eurytus and his sons, takes the city, pillages it, and leads Iole away captive.
is_by Deianira [by hanging] Deianira learns what has happened to Hercules after he wears the treated tunic. She hangs herself.
Antiope, Nycteus’s daughter, becomes pregnant by Zeus, flees and marries Epopeus, is punished and abused by Lycus and Dirce, then is recognized and rescued by her sons Zethus and Amphion.

The sons of Hercules are a group who flee Eurystheus after Hercules is translated to the gods, seek protection with Ceyx and Athens, and, after Eurystheus is killed, come to the Peloponnese and seize all its cities.
Athenians protect Hercules' sons by refusing Eurystheus' demand, wage war in their defense, and kill his sons Alexander, Iphimedon, Eurybius, Mentor, and Perimedes.

is_fought_by Athenians [against Eurystheus] The Athenians undertook the war with Eurystheus because they refused to surrender the sons of Hercules. During the conflict, the Athenians killed Eurystheus's sons.

The Heraclids, sons of Hercules, flee Eurystheus and seek protection in Athens. They attack the Peloponnese but withdraw to Marathon after plague and an oracle say they returned too early. Under Oxylus they later defeat the Peloponnesians by land and sea, kill Tisamenus, seize all cities, and divide them by lot, ending Inachus’s family.

l: oracle concerning the Heraclids' return, The Library
s: Oracle concerning the Heraclids' return warns against a premature return, marked by plague in Peloponnese and Hippotes' ten-year banishment; it requires the third crop, explained as the third generation, and identifies the narrows as the broad-bellied sea right of the Isthmus.
Tisamenus, son of Orestes, is reigning over the Peloponnesians when the Heraclids make an attempt to return. He is later killed by them after they defeat the enemy by land and sea.

builds Naupactus ships [in Locris] Temenus and his brothers consult the oracle about their return. He blames the god for their earlier misfortunes, then prepares the army, builds ships at Naupactus, and later receives Argos in the division of the conquered Peloponnese. His sons arrange his murder because he favors Hyrnetho and Deiphontes.

is_married_to Cresphontes's wife Merope [before his murder] Cresphontes uses a clod of earth instead of a stone in the drawing of lots so that he will receive Messene. He is later murdered with two of his sons after reigning there for a short time.
Aristodemus marries Argia, fathers twin sons Eurysthenes and Procles, and is killed by a thunderbolt at Naupactus.

Naupactus is the place in Locris where Temenus builds ships for the expedition. The army suffers a calamity there when the soothsayer is killed, the ships are destroyed, and the land force is overcome by famine.

is_defeated_by Peloponnesians [at Naupactus through famine and destruction of the fleet] Aristodemus's army suffers disaster at Naupactus after Hippotes kills the soothsayer. Its ships are destroyed, its land force suffers famine, and the army disbands.

is_a soothsayer [an Acarnanian] The soothsayer Carnus appears among the army, reciting oracles in a state of inspiration. The army mistakes him for a magician sent by the Peloponnesians, and Hippotes kills him with a javelin.
Hippotes, son of Phylas, kills the soothsayer Carnus with a javelin after mistaking him for an enemy agent; an oracle links the army’s calamity to it, and he is banished for ten years.

is_identified_as Oxylus [interpreted through the oracle] The oracle commands the Heraclids to take the Three-eyed One as their guide. They interpret this instruction through Oxylus, who is found riding a one-eyed horse.
The Peloponnesians defeat the Heraclids in an earlier battle and kill Aristomachus. They later lose to the Heraclids by land and sea under Oxylus's guidance.
Heraclids conquer the Peloponnese by defeating enemies on land and sea and killing Tisamenus, then establish altars and divide cities by lots.

l: drawing of lots for the cities, The Library
s: After conquering the Peloponnese, the leaders sacrifice and draw lots: Temenus receives Argos first, the sons of Aristodemus Lacedaemon second, and Cresphontes obtains Messene third through a dissolving clod.
Hyrnetho is Temenus's daughter, and Temenus favors her and her husband Deiphontes over his sons. After Temenus's murder, the army assigns the kingdom to Hyrnetho and Deiphontes.
Deiphontes is Hyrnetho's husband and is favored by Temenus. After Temenus is murdered, the army decides that the kingdom belongs to Deiphontes and Hyrnetho.
Merope is the wife of the murdered Cresphontes. Polyphontes takes her as his wife against her will, but she saves her third son Aepytus by sending him to her own father to be raised.

is_married_to Cresphontes's wife Merope [against her will] Polyphontes, one of the true Heraclids, takes Merope as his wife after Cresphontes's murder and becomes king. Aepytus later secretly returns and kills him.
Aepytus, Merope's third son raised by his maternal grandfather, reaches manhood, secretly returns, kills Polyphontes, and recovers his fathers' kingdom.
is_committed Cresphontes [with two of his sons] Cresphontes is murdered with two of his sons after he has ruled Messene for a short time. Polyphontes then takes Merope and the kingship.
is_committed Polyphontes [by Aepytus] Polyphontes is secretly killed by Aepytus after Aepytus reaches manhood and returns. Aepytus then recovers the kingdom of his fathers.

l: return of the Heraclids, The Library
s: is_delayed_by plague in Peloponnese [because it occurred before the proper time] The Heraclids' first return causes a plague because it occurs before the proper time. After failed attempts and a corrected interpretation of the oracle, they return under Oxylus's guidance and conquer the Peloponnese.
The family of Inachus is a genealogy extending from Belus to the Heraclids, described before the account turns to Agenor's house.
The unit begins the account of the house of Agenor after describing the family of Inachus.
Telephassa married Agenor, bore Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, and accompanied the search for Europa.
Phoenix was a son of Agenor and Telephassa. He was sent with his brothers to search for Europa.
Cilix was a son of Agenor and Telephassa. He was sent with his brothers to search for Europa.
The bull was Zeus in transformed form. As a tame bull, it carried Europa across the sea to Crete.
The search for Europa began after she disappeared. Agenor ordered his sons to search for her and not return until they found her, and Telephassa accompanied them.
The sons of Agenor, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, were sent to search for Europa after her disappearance. Agenor ordered them not to return until they found her, and Telephassa went with them.

Althaemenes left Crete with his sister Apemosyne because he feared becoming his father’s murderer. In Rhodes he later killed Catreus unknowingly, then disappeared into a chasm after learning what he had done.
Polyidus, son of Coeranus and a diviner, identifies Minos’s cow, finds and restores dead Glaucus with an herb, then is compelled to teach him divination.

Harmonia, daughter of Aphrodite and Ares, is given by Zeus in marriage to Cadmus and receives a robe and necklace made by Hephaestus. She leaves Thebes with Cadmus for the Encheleans, leads them against the Illyrians, then becomes a serpent and is sent to the Elysian Fields.
Semele, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, is secretly loved by Zeus and later named Thyone by Dionysus after being brought from Hades.
Polydorus becomes king of Thebes, marries Nycteis, and fathers Labdacus.
Actaeon, son of Autonoe and Aristaeus, trained by Chiron as a hunter, sees Artemis bathing, becomes a deer, and is killed by his own dogs.
The Labyrinth was constructed by Daedalus and had tangled passages that confused the way out. Minos shut the Minotaur inside it and guarded him there.
The Sparti are armed men sprung from dragon’s teeth; after emerging from the ground, they fight and kill one another, leaving five survivors.
The Minotaur, born to Pasiphae after she joined Minos’s bull with Daedalus’s assistance, has a bull’s face and human body; Minos confines it in the Labyrinth in accordance with oracles.

guards spring of Ares [at the spring used for water] A dragon guarded the spring of Ares and killed most of the men sent by Cadmus to fetch water. Cadmus killed it, and Athena advised him to sow its teeth.

Polynices carries the necklace and robe to Argos and gives the necklace to Eriphyle. Eriphyle accepts it and persuades Amphiaraus to join the war. The necklace of Eriphyle was given by Alcmaeon to Arsinoe after his purification by Phegeus. Alcmaeon later obtained it again by claiming that it had to be dedicated at Delphi, and his sons eventually dedicated it there according to Achelous's instruction.

involves Zeus [Zeus conveys Europa to Crete] The abduction of Europa occurred when Zeus, disguised as a tame bull, carried her over the sea to Crete. Her brothers and others searched for her but could not find her and settled in different places.

l: birth of the Minotaur, The Library
s: results_from Pasiphae [after mating with the bull through the wooden cow] The birth of the Minotaur followed Poseidon’s punishment of Minos for failing to sacrifice the bull. Daedalus built a wooden cow for Pasiphae, who joined with the bull and gave birth to Asterius, called the Minotaur.

The foundation of Thebes began when Cadmus followed a cow in accordance with the oracle at Delphi. After the cow collapsed, Cadmus killed the dragon guarding the spring of Ares and established the city there.

l: sowing of the dragon’s teeth, The Library
s: produces Sparti [armed men rising from the ground] The sowing of the dragon’s teeth was performed by Cadmus on Athena’s advice. The teeth produced armed men, who became the Sparti and fought one another.

l: death and resurrection of Glaucus, The Library
s: involves Polyidus [Polyidus restores Glaucus to life] Glaucus died after falling into a jar of honey while chasing a mouse. Polyidus saw a serpent revive another serpent with an herb, applied the herb to Glaucus, and restored him to life.

is_caused_by Artemis [in the account where Actaeon sees her bathing] Actaeon’s death followed his seeing Artemis bathing, according to the more common account. Artemis changed him into a deer and caused his dogs to become mad and devour him.

l: marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia, The Library
s: The marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia took place after Cadmus had completed his service to Ares. Zeus gave Harmonia to Cadmus, and the gods attended the wedding and celebrated it with hymns.
Bacchanals accompanying Dionysus are captured with Satyrs by Lycurgus, suddenly released, and compelled into Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron.

Pentheus, son of Agave and Echion, succeeds Cadmus in the kingdom and opposes the Bacchic rites. He spies on the Bacchanals at Cithaeron, where Agave, mad and mistaking him for a wild beast, tears him apart.
Tyrrhenian pirates hire a trireme to ferry Dionysus from Icaria to Naxos but plan to sell him in Asia; after Dionysus transforms the ship, they go mad, leap into the sea, and become dolphins.
Encheleans, attacked by Illyrians, receive an oracle, appoint Cadmus and Harmonia as leaders, and defeat the Illyrians.
The Illyrians attack the Encheleans but are defeated when the Encheleans are led by Cadmus and Harmonia. Cadmus then reigns over them.
is_son_of Chthonius Nycteus is the son of Chthonius and the father of Nycteis and Antiope. He commands Lycus to punish Epopeus and Antiope, then kills himself in distress.
Labdacus, born to Polydorus and Nycteis, shared Pentheus’s outlook and died after him, leaving one-year-old Laius.

Laius, son of Labdacus, was left a one-year-old child, ruled over by Lycus, and expelled from Thebes by Zethus and Amphion. In the Peloponnese Pelops received him; he carried off Chrysippus. After Amphion died, Laius became king of Thebes and married Menoeceus’s daughter. Despite an oracle, he fathered Oedipus, who killed him in Phocis.

Zethus, son of Antiope and Zeus, is exposed and raised by a neatherd, tends cattle, reunites with Antiope, kills Lycus and Dirce, expels Laius, fortifies and succeeds to Thebes with Amphion, and marries Thebe.
Dirce, wife of Lycus, mistreats imprisoned Antiope until Zethus and Amphion bind her to a bull, kill her, and name a spring for her.
is_between Encheleans [the Encheleans are attacked] The Illyrian war is fought when the Illyrians attack the Encheleans. The Encheleans, led by Cadmus and Harmonia, defeat the Illyrians.

l: Cadmus's and Harmonia's departure from Thebes, The Library
s: Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes for the Encheleans, then lead the Encheleans against the Illyrians.

l: Cadmus's reign over the Illyrians, The Library
s: has_ruler Cadmus After leading the Encheleans to victory over the Illyrians, Cadmus reigns over the Illyrians. Illyrius is born to him during this reign.
After killing Lycus and Dirce, Zethus and Amphion take over the sovereignty and fortify Thebes. The stones follow Amphion's lyre as the city is fortified.

dies_by hanging [after the secret of Oedipus's parentage came to light] Jocasta was identified by some as the daughter of Menoeceus whom Laius married. She unknowingly married her son Oedipus, and after the hidden truth was revealed, she hanged herself.

Oedipus, exposed as an infant after Laius pierced his ankles and raised by Periboea, leaves Corinth believing his nominal parents are his own. Destined to kill Laius and marry Jocasta, he kills Laius and Polyphontes, solves the Sphinx’s riddle, rules Thebes, and unknowingly marries Jocasta. They have Polynices, Eteocles, Ismene, and Antigone. After the truth emerges, he blinds himself, is expelled, and dies at Colonus.

Sphinx is a monster, daughter of Echidna and Typhon, with a woman’s face, lion’s breast, feet and tail, and bird’s wings. She occupies Mount Phicium, where she poses a riddle learned from the Muses to the Thebans and devours failures. After Oedipus solves it, she falls from the citadel of Thebes and dies.

l: riddle of the Sphinx, The Library
s: The riddle asked what has one voice and becomes four-footed, two-footed, and three-footed. Oedipus answered that it was a human being, who crawls on four limbs as an infant, walks on two feet as an adult, and uses a staff as a third support in old age.

Polynices, son of Oedipus, is a claimant to Thebes's kingdom. He agrees with Eteocles to alternate rule, but Eteocles refuses to surrender power, so Polynices is banished and goes to Argos with a necklace and robe. He marries Argia, helps bring champions toward war, and demands the kingdom. Stationed at Hypsistan Gate, he fights Eteocles in single combat; they kill each other. Creon leaves Polynices unburied until Antigone secretly buries him.

Eteocles is a Theban leader who makes a compact with Polynices to rule the kingdom in alternate years. He rules first in one account but refuses to surrender the kingdom when asked. He arms and organizes the Thebans against the Argives, then fights Polynices in single combat for Thebes; the brothers kill each other.
Antigone, Oedipus’s daughter, secretly steals and buries Polynices’ body; Creon discovers her and buries her alive in a grave.

Niobe's children are a group listed here as seven sons and seven daughters, including Ethodaia, Cleodoxa, Astyoche, Phthia, Pelopia, Astycratia, and Ogygia. Artemis killed the daughters and Apollo the sons, though accounts differ on survivors and total numbers.

The kingdom is to be ruled by Eteocles and Polynices in alternate years. Eteocles refuses to hand it over to Polynices after his period of rule. The kingdom of Thebes is contested by Eteocles and Polynices in a single combat. The contest ends with both of them dead.
Capaneus attacks the Ogygian Gate, climbs its walls by ladder, and Zeus strikes him with a thunderbolt, prompting Argive flight.

Melanion pursues and defeats Atalanta in a marriage race using Aphrodite’s golden apples, marries her, and fathers Parthenopaeus in one account; after intercourse with Atalanta in Zeus’s precinct, both are transformed into lions.

The Seven Champions are Adrastus’s seven leaders for war against Thebes. With variant membership, they march via Nemea, bury the slain Opheltes, and send Tydeus to demand that Eteocles yield the kingdom.
kills Opheltes [while Hypsipyle shows the spring] A serpent kills Opheltes while Hypsipyle is showing the champions the spring. Adrastus and his companions kill the serpent.

After Archemorus’s burial, the champions establish the Nemean Games in honor of Opheltes, called Archemorus; Adrastus, Eteoclus, Tydeus, Amphiaraus, Laodocus, Polynices, and Parthenopaeus win seven contests.

Adrastus gathers the Seven Champions for the war against Thebes. Amphiaraus initially opposes the expedition because he foresees the deaths of its participants except Adrastus, but Eriphyle persuades him to join; the army later proceeds toward Thebes.
Chariclo, a nymph dear to Athena and mother of Tiresias, asks Athena to restore Tiresias’s sight after his blinding.

l: Argive attack on Thebes, The Library
s: The Argive attack began with the Argives arming themselves and approaching the walls of Thebes. Seven named Argive leaders were assigned to the seven gates.

l: battle between the Argives and Thebans, The Library
s: The battle between the Cadmeans and Argives begins with Argives taking positions at the gates as Eteocles arms and organizes Thebans. Cadmeans are driven to the walls, but Zeus strikes Capaneus; the Argives flee, and Eteocles and Polynices fight over the kingdom.

Different accounts explain the blindness of Tiresias. One says that Athena blinded him after he saw her naked; another says that Hera blinded him after he answered her dispute with Zeus about sexual pleasure.

l: prophetic power of Tiresias, The Library
s: Tiresias possessed prophetic power despite his blindness. Athena is said to have enabled him to understand every bird's voice, and Zeus is said to have granted him the power of divination.
occurs_at gates of Thebes The self-sacrifice of Menoeceus consists of his offering himself to Ares by killing himself before the gates. Tiresias says that it will bring victory to the Thebans.
are_chased_to walls of Thebes [in the battle] The Cadmeans are driven in pursuit as far as the walls during the battle. Their opponents subsequently turn to flee after Zeus strikes Capaneus.

l: single combat of Eteocles and Polynices, The Library
s: concerns kingdom of Thebes The single combat of Eteocles and Polynices is fought by agreement of both armies over the kingdom. Each brother kills the other.

remain_unburied unburied bodies [by Creon’s order] The Argive dead were denied burial by Creon. At the appeal of Adrastus, the Athenians under Theseus recovered them and gave them to their relatives for burial.

The Epigoni first ravaged the villages around Thebes and then fought the Thebans under Laodamas. After Laodamas was killed, the Thebans fled, the Argives entered Thebes, took its booty, and destroyed its walls.

The robe of Eriphyle was given by Thersander to Eriphyle and influenced her to persuade her sons to join the war. Alcmaeon later gave it to Arsinoe, falsely claimed that he needed it for dedication at Delphi, and ultimately had it dedicated there by his sons according to Achelous's instruction.

Phegeus purified Alcmaeon at Psophis and gave him his daughter Arsinoe in marriage. He believed Alcmaeon's claim that the necklace and robe were needed for dedication at Delphi, but ordered his sons to kill Alcmaeon after learning that he intended to give them to Callirrhoe.

is_colonized_by Alcmaeon [with settlers gathered in Epirus] Acarnania was colonized by the sons of Alcmaeon after they avenged their father's death and dedicated the necklace and robe at Delphi according to Achelous's instruction.
Lycaon, son of Pelasgus and king of the Arcadians, fathers fifty sons; after his sons prepare an impious banquet, Zeus destroys him with a thunderbolt.

succeeds_to_kingdom Lycaon Nyctimus is the youngest of Lycaon’s sons and is spared when Zeus destroys Lycaon and the other sons. He succeeds to the kingdom, and the flood of Deucalion occurs during his reign.
Maenalus is one of Lycaon’s sons and is identified as the elder brother who advises the preparation of the impious sacrifice for Zeus.

Callisto is described as a nymph or daughter of Lycaon, Nycteus, or Ceteus. Artemis’s companion, she wears Artemis’s garb and vows virginity. Zeus sleeps with her against her will; to escape Hera’s notice, he transforms her into a bear and later places her among the stars.

Lycaon’s sons are described as surpassing all people in pride and impiety. Zeus tests their impiety, and their treatment of him at the banquet leads to the destruction of Lycaon and his sons; some accounts also connect their impiety with Deucalion’s flood.
Arcas, spouse of Leanira, Meganira, or Chrysopelia in differing genealogies, fathers Elatus and Aphidas, who divide the land while Elatus holds power.
Aphidas, son of Arcas and Leaneira and brother of Elatus, fathered Aleus and Stheneboea.

requires wooers [to race against Atalanta for the right to marry her] Atalanta's wooers raced from a starting point while she pursued them in armor. A wooer who was caught was to die, while one who escaped was to marry her; after many had died, Melanion won by using golden apples.
Atalanta's wooers race her for marriage; those caught die, and many perish before Melanion enters and wins.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable has title Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable has author Thomas Bulfinch

s: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable has date 1855

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable has source class canonical

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Ceyx is a king (of Thessaly)
q: Ceyx was King of Thessaly, where he reigned in peace without violence or wrong.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Halcyone is a daughter of Aeolus
q: Halcyone, the daughter of Aeolus, was his wife, and devotedly attached to him.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Halcyone is a wife of Ceyx (devotedly attached to him)
q: Halcyone, the daughter of Aeolus, was his wife, and devotedly attached to him.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Halcyone shudders at his intention
q: But as soon as he disclosed his intention to his wife Halcyone, a shudder ran through her frame, and her face grew deadly pale.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Halcyone is transformed into birds (with Ceyx, by the pitying gods)
q: But indeed he did feel it, and by the pitying gods both of them were changed into birds.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable
s: Halcyone broods over her nest (for seven placid days, in winter time)
q: For seven placid days, in winter time, Halcyone broods over her nest, which floats upon the sea.
